Clinical Research Examples with jSurvival

ClinicoPath Development Team

Source: vignettes/03-clinical-examples.Rmd
03-clinical-examples.Rmd

Overview

This vignette provides practical examples of using jSurvival for common clinical research scenarios. Each example demonstrates a workflow from data preparation to interpretation of results. The data are simulated by the code shown here, so the code runs as written, and the simulated data are not meant to show any real effect. In your own data, columns can be passed as names, as below, or as quoted text.

Example 1: Cancer Treatment Comparison Study

Background

A clinical trial comparing two cancer treatments (Treatment A vs. Treatment B) with overall survival as the primary endpoint.

Research Question

Is there a significant difference in overall survival between Treatment A and Treatment B?

Data Structure 

# Example data structure
library(jsurvival)
set.seed(1)
cancer_data <- data.frame(
  PatientID = 1:200,
  Treatment = rep(c("Treatment A", "Treatment B"), each = 100),
  OS_months = c(rnorm(100, 24, 8), rnorm(100, 30, 10)),
  Death = rbinom(200, 1, 0.6),
  Age = rnorm(200, 65, 10),
  Stage = sample(c("I", "II", "III", "IV"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  ECOG = sample(0:2, 200, replace = TRUE)
)

Analysis Steps

Step 1: Single Arm Analysis (Overall Population) 

# First, examine overall survival characteristics
singlearm_result <- singlearm(
  data = cancer_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  cutp = "12, 24, 36",
  timetypeoutput = "months"
)

Interpretation: - Median overall survival for the entire cohort - 1, 2, and 3-year survival rates - 95% confidence intervals for all estimates

Step 2: Treatment Comparison 

# Compare survival between treatments
survival_result <- survival(
  data = cancer_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Treatment,
  analysistype = "overall",
  ph_cox = TRUE,   # also test the proportional hazards assumption
  sc = TRUE,       # draw the Kaplan-Meier plot
  ci95 = TRUE,
  risktable = TRUE
)

Key Outputs: - Log-rank test p-value for treatment difference - Hazard ratio comparing Treatment B vs. Treatment A - Kaplan-Meier curves with risk tables - Median survival times by treatment group

Step 3: Multivariable Analysis 

# Adjust for potential confounders
multi_result <- multisurvival(
  data = cancer_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = c("Treatment", "Stage", "ECOG"),
  contexpl = "Age"
)

Interpretation: - Adjusted hazard ratio for treatment effect - Factors associated with the outcome after adjustment - Model fit statistics (concordance index, an apparent value that is optimistic)

Clinical Interpretation

If HR = 0.75 (95% CI: 0.60-0.95), p = 0.02: - Treatment B is associated with a 25% lower hazard of death compared to Treatment A - This result is statistically significant - The confidence interval excludes 1.0, supporting the treatment benefit

Example 2: Biomarker Cut-point Analysis

Background

Investigating whether a continuous biomarker is associated with patient outcomes and deriving a candidate threshold.

Research Question

What cut-point for Biomarker X best separates overall survival in this dataset, and does it hold in independent data?

Analysis Workflow

Step 1: Continuous Variable Analysis 

# Simulated data for this example
biomarker_data <- data.frame(
  OS_months = rexp(150, rate = 1 / 30),
  Death = rbinom(150, 1, 0.6),
  Biomarker_X = rlnorm(150, meanlog = 2.5, sdlog = 0.5)
)

# Find a data-derived cut-point for the biomarker
biomarker_result <- survivalcont(
  data = biomarker_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  contexpl = Biomarker_X,
  findcut = TRUE,
  cutp = "12, 36, 60"
)

Outputs: - Data-derived cut-point value, with an adjusted p-value that allows for the search over cut-points - Hazard ratio per one-unit increase in the biomarker - Median survival and survival rates for the high and low groups

Step 2: Report the cut-off, and validate it elsewhere 

# Validation data must be independent: patients who played no part in choosing the
# cut-point. Testing the cut-point in the data that chose it confirms it by construction.
validation_data <- data.frame(
  OS_months = rexp(120, rate = 1 / 30),
  Death = rbinom(120, 1, 0.6),
  Biomarker_X = rlnorm(120, meanlog = 2.5, sdlog = 0.5)
)
# Freeze the exact discovery cutoff, including its equality convention.
discovery_cutoff <- biomarker_result$rescutTable$asDF$cutpoint[1]
stopifnot(length(discovery_cutoff) == 1L, is.finite(discovery_cutoff))
validation_data$Biomarker_High <- ifelse(
  validation_data$Biomarker_X > discovery_cutoff, "High", "Low")

validation_result <- survival(
  data = validation_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Biomarker_High,
  ph_cox = TRUE
)

Clinical Translation

If optimal cut-point = 15.2 ng/mL, HR = 2.1 (95% CI: 1.4-3.2): - Patients with biomarker >15.2 ng/mL have 2.1 times the fitted hazard compared with those at or below 15.2 in this hypothetical grouped analysis. This group contrast differs from the HR per one-unit biomarker increase; a discovery-cohort group HR is optimistic. - Validate the threshold in an independent cohort before any clinical use - This is an association, not a causal effect

Example 3: Time-to-Event Analysis with Competing Risks

Background

Studying cancer-specific mortality while accounting for deaths from other causes.

Research Question

What factors predict cancer-specific death, considering other-cause mortality as a competing risk?

Analysis Approach 

# Simulated data for this example
competing_data <- data.frame(
  OS_months = rexp(200, rate = 1 / 30),
  Treatment = sample(c("Treatment A", "Treatment B"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  death_cause = sample(c("Alive", "Cancer", "Other"), 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.4, 0.2))
)
competing_data$Death_cancer <- as.numeric(competing_data$death_cause == "Cancer")
competing_data$Death_other <- as.numeric(competing_data$death_cause == "Other")

# For competing risks, use cause-specific outcomes
# Death_cancer: 1 = cancer death, 0 = alive or other death
# Death_other: 1 = other death, 0 = alive or cancer death

# Cancer-specific survival analysis
cancer_specific <- survival(
  data = competing_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death_cancer,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Treatment,
  analysistype = "overall",
  ph_cox = TRUE
)

# Other-cause mortality analysis
other_cause <- survival(
  data = competing_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death_other,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Treatment,
  analysistype = "overall",
  ph_cox = TRUE
)

Interpretation: - Separate hazard ratios for cancer-specific and other-cause mortality - Treatment effects may differ between competing outcomes - For cumulative incidence use the competing-risk mode of Survival Analysis (Analysis type: Competing Risk); for regression, Multivariable Survival fits a Fine-Gray model.

Example 4: Landmark Analysis

Background

Addressing guarantee-time bias when analyzing post-treatment biomarkers or response markers.

Research Question

Does tumor response at 3 months predict long-term survival?

Analysis Strategy 

# Simulated data for this example
original_data <- data.frame(
  OS_months = rexp(200, rate = 1 / 30),
  Death = rbinom(200, 1, 0.6),
  Response_3month = sample(c("Responder", "Non-responder"), 200, replace = TRUE)
)

# jsurvival applies the landmark itself: pass the ORIGINAL time column. It keeps
# patients still under observation after 3 months and restarts the clock there.
landmark_result <- survival(
  data = original_data, elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death, outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Response_3month,
  uselandmark = TRUE, landmark = 3
)

Key Points: - Only includes patients with follow-up time longer than the landmark; a patient whose time equals the landmark exactly is excluded - Do not shift the time column yourself as well, or time is shifted twice - Addresses guarantee-time bias for a marker known by the landmark time - Useful for post-treatment predictors

Example 5: Dose-Response Analysis

Background

Evaluating survival outcomes across different dose levels of a treatment.

Research Question

Is there a dose-response relationship for treatment efficacy?

Analysis Steps

Step 1: Categorical Dose Analysis 

# Simulated data for this example
dose_data <- data.frame(
  OS_months = rexp(240, rate = 1 / 30),
  Death = rbinom(240, 1, 0.6),
  Dose_category = factor(sample(c("Low", "Medium", "High"), 240, replace = TRUE),
                         levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
)

# Treat dose as categorical variable
dose_categorical <- survival(
  data = dose_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Dose_category,  # Low, Medium, High
  pw = TRUE,
  padjustmethod = "holm"
)

Step 2: Trend Analysis 

# Test for linear trend across dose levels
# Create ordinal dose variable (1, 2, 3)
dose_data$Dose_ordinal <- as.numeric(factor(dose_data$Dose_category, 
                                           levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")))

trend_result <- multisurvival(
  data = dose_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  contexpl = "Dose_ordinal"
)

Interpretation: - Test for overall dose effect (3-group comparison) - Test for linear trend: the ordinal dose goes in Continuous Explanatory Variable, because survival() treats a numeric explanatory variable as categorical - HR per dose level

Example 6: Propensity Score Matching

Background

Comparing treatments in observational data while reducing confounding by measured baseline variables. Unmeasured confounding remains.

Research Question

What is the treatment effect after accounting for baseline differences between groups?

Analysis Workflow 

# Step 1: Create matched dataset (outside jSurvival)
# Here cancer_data stands in for a matched dataset.
matched_data <- cancer_data

# Step 2: Analyze matched cohort
matched_result <- survival(
  data = matched_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = Treatment,
  analysistype = "overall",
  ph_cox = TRUE
)

# Step 3: Sensitivity analysis with additional adjustment
sensitivity_result <- multisurvival(
  data = matched_data,
  elapsedtime = OS_months,
  outcome = Death,
  outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  explanatory = "Treatment",
  contexpl = "Age"
)

Reporting Guidelines

Essential Elements

  1. Study Design: Clearly describe cohort and follow-up
  2. Sample Size: Total patients, events, median follow-up
  3. Statistical Methods: Analysis approach and software used
  4. Results Presentation:
    • Median survival with 95% CI
    • Hazard ratios with 95% CI
    • P-values and statistical tests used
    • Kaplan-Meier curves with risk tables

Example Results Section

“Among [N] patients (Treatment A: n=[n], Treatment B: n=[n]), there were [events] deaths during a median follow-up of [time] months (IQR: [Q1]-[Q3]). Median overall survival was [median] months (95% CI: [lower]-[upper]) for Treatment A versus [median] months (95% CI: [lower]-[upper]) for Treatment B. Treatment B was associated with a [percent]% [lower or higher] hazard of death compared to Treatment A (HR=[HR], 95% CI: [lower]-[upper], p=[p]). The 2-year survival rates were [rate]% (95% CI: [lower]-[upper]%) and [rate]% (95% CI: [lower]-[upper]%) for Treatment A and B, respectively.”

Figure Legends

“Figure 1. Kaplan-Meier survival curves comparing Treatment A versus Treatment B. The table below shows the number of patients at risk at each time point. P-value from log-rank test. HR: hazard ratio, CI: confidence interval.”

Common Pitfalls and Solutions

Pitfall 1: Immortal Time Bias

Problem: Including post-baseline events as baseline predictors Solution: Use landmark analysis, or time-dependent covariates (outside jSurvival)

Pitfall 2: Multiple Testing

Problem: Testing multiple endpoints without adjustment Solution: Use appropriate p-value correction methods

Pitfall 3: Proportional Hazards Violation

Problem: HR changes over time Solution: Use stratified Cox models, or time-dependent effects (outside jSurvival)

Pitfall 4: Insufficient Follow-up

Problem: High censoring rates affect reliability Solution: Report median follow-up and censoring patterns

Conclusion

These examples show how jSurvival applies to common clinical research questions. The key to successful survival analysis is:

  1. Clear research questions with appropriate study design
  2. Careful data preparation and quality control
  3. Appropriate statistical methods for the research context
  4. Complete reporting following established guidelines
  5. Clinical interpretation that considers both statistical and practical significance

For additional support and examples, visit the jSurvival website and ClinicoPath documentation.
